action_criteria.expected_evidence: Collapsing weakness of right finger extension and variable resistance to passive extension, with no sensory trick and no skin, temperature or swelling change
action_criteria.label: Examine the fixed posture for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: A fixed flexed posture of the right wrist and fingers within 2 days of a minor injury: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as collapsing weakness and variable resistance to passive movement, and on the absence of a sensory trick, task specificity, autonomic or trophic change and other neurological signs, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B; Schrag 2004).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No dopamine-blocking drug on the list, against an acute dystonic reaction; bleeding risk of the SSRI with the NSAID
action_criteria.label: Review his medicines for a drug cause of the dystonia
action_criteria.rationale: He started sertraline a week before the posture appeared; dopamine receptor antagonists cause acute dystonic reactions and SSRIs rarely cause dystonia, so his medicines are reviewed before the posture is attributed to a functional disorder, and he also takes ibuprofen with the SSRI.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No basal ganglia or other structural lesion
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, once, if a structural question remains
action_criteria.rationale: A basal ganglia lesion can cause a hemidystonia, but the posture is confined to one hand after a peripheral injury and there is no other neurological sign; one non-contrast MRI is acceptable but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies post-traumatic stress, anxiety and mood to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify his post-traumatic stress, anxiety and mood to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
Immobilize the hand in a cast or splint for the fixed posture.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional fixed dystonia of the right hand) based on collapsing weakness of right finger extension and variable resistance to passive extension that increases with attempted movement, in a posture fixed at rest from onset after a minor injury, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus) and for occupational therapy for use of the right hand, without immobilization.
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid PTSD with trauma-focused psychological therapy.

avoided_actions.rationale: He has had no loss of consciousness, syncope or palpitations; an ECG answers no question about a fixed hand posture.
There is no murmur, syncope or embolic question; an echocardiogram answers nothing in this patient.
There are no palpitations or syncope; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
There is no head injury and no sign beyond the right hand; a head CT adds radiation and no information.
He is afebrile with no inflammatory, encephalopathic or neuropathic feature; a lumbar puncture would add risk and change nothing.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in a functional dystonia and answers no question in this patient.
Sensation is normal in the median, ulnar and radial territories and the flexion posture is not the pattern of a nerve palsy; nerve conduction studies and EMG have no question to answer.
Sensation is normal in both hands; somatosensory evoked potentials answer no question here.

There is no bradykinesia, rest tremor or rigidity outside the fixed hand, and a posture fixed since a minor injury is not a question of presynaptic dopaminergic loss; a dopamine transporter scan answers nothing.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — functional fixed dystonia of the right hand

differential.diagnosis: Complex regional pain syndrome, possibly coexisting
differential.key_features: Pain and a fixed posture after a minor injury, and fixed dystonia overlaps with CRPS; but there is no color, temperature, sweating, swelling or trophic change and no allodynia or hyperalgesia, so the Budapest criteria are not met. Watch for these signs.

Focal dystonia is mobile and task-specific at onset and may respond to a sensory trick; this posture has been fixed at rest from the start, began within 2 days of an injury, and has no sensory trick or task specificity.
Sertraline was started a week before onset, but SSRI-associated dystonia is rare, no dopamine receptor antagonist has been taken, and the posture did not change when the dose was increased.
The posture is confined to one hand after a peripheral injury, with no other dystonic, pyramidal or sensory sign.

key_clinical_evidence: Collapsing weakness of right finger extension and variable resistance to passive extension that increases with attempted movement are positive signs.

A posture fixed at rest from onset, within 2 days of a minor peripheral injury, with no sensory trick or task specificity, is the pattern of fixed dystonia (Schrag 2004), not of primary focal dystonia.
No color, temperature, sweating, swelling or trophic change and no allodynia: the Budapest criteria for CRPS are not met, although CRPS can coexist and is watched for.
No dopamine receptor antagonist has been taken, so there is no acute dystonic reaction, and sertraline is an unlikely cause.
PTSD after witnessing a fatal accident 8 weeks ago is a treatment target and supportive context; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A minor peripheral injury is a common trigger of functional fixed dystonia; normal sensation in every nerve territory and the absence of swelling or trophic change leave no structural question, and immobilization worsens the posture.
red_herrings.data_point: Bruised right wrist on a door 5 weeks ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Look for a structural wrist or nerve injury with nerve conduction studies, EMG or imaging, or immobilize the wrist

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: SSRI-associated dystonia is rare, the posture did not change when the dose was increased, and no dopamine receptor antagonist was taken; sertraline treats his PTSD.
red_herrings.data_point: Sertraline started a week before the posture appeared
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the posture to the SSRI and stop it, leaving his PTSD untreated

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The trauma is supportive context and a treatment target, not a substitute for the positive signs of the examination.
red_herrings.data_point: PTSD after witnessing a fatal road accident 8 weeks ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the trauma alone, without positive signs

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional dystonia: collapsing weakness of right finger extension and variable resistance to passive extension that increases with attempted movement, in a posture fixed at rest since onset. No sensory trick or task specificity, no color, temperature, swelling or trophic change in the hand, and no other neurological sign.

interactions: Sertraline with ibuprofen: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin and NSAIDs injure the gastric mucosa; increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding with regular combined use. Consider gastroprotection or a non-NSAID analgesic.
current_medications.proposed: Sertraline 100 mg once daily; ibuprofen 400 mg as needed, up to three times daily
current_medications.summary: One moderate interaction (sertraline with ibuprofen, gastrointestinal bleeding risk). No dopamine receptor antagonist among the current medicines.
warnings: Sertraline: dystonia and other extrapyramidal reactions have been reported rarely with SSRIs, usually soon after starting or increasing the dose.
No dopamine receptor antagonist (antipsychotic, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) is among the current medicines.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case: a painful fixed flexed posture of the right wrist and fingers within 2 days of a minor injury, in a young man with PTSD who started sertraline a week before.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: The required work-up is the examination, which finds collapsing weakness and variable resistance to passive movement, with no sign of CRPS; a medicine review is recommended. The injury invites nerve studies and immobilization, the recent SSRI invites stopping his PTSD treatment, and the pain invites a CRPS label without its signs.

patient.history_present_illness: A 22-year-old right-handed restaurant manager is admitted from the emergency department with a painful, fixed bent posture of the right wrist and fingers. Five weeks ago he bruised the back of his right wrist on a swing door at work; there was no wound and he kept working. Within 2 days the wrist and fingers drew into a flexed position that he cannot straighten, and it has not changed since, at rest, at night or when he tries to use the hand. Attempts to straighten it are painful. He cannot hold cutlery, write or use a phone with the right hand, has been off work for 4 weeks, and came to the emergency department because the pain was keeping him awake. He has noticed no weakness or numbness elsewhere, no change in skin color, temperature or sweating of the hand, no swelling, no neck pain and no other abnormal movement. Eight weeks ago he witnessed a fatal road accident outside the restaurant and gave first aid at the scene; since then he has had nightmares and flashbacks and avoids the street where it happened. His general practitioner started sertraline 50 mg 6 weeks ago and increased it to 100 mg 3 weeks ago; the posture did not change with the dose increase. He takes ibuprofen as needed for the wrist pain and has taken no other medicines.

neurological_exam.additional: No sensory trick changes the posture, and it does not vary with task, at rest, on reaching or on attempted writing.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose normal on the left; on the right limited by the posture, without dysmetria of the arm. Heel-to-shin normal bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal, including eye movements, facial movements and speech; no facial or neck dystonia.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait; the right arm is held flexed against the body with reduced arm swing.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented, tense and tearful when describing the accident. Speech fluent. Attention and memory intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Right wrist held in fixed flexion with the fingers flexed at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints and the thumb adducted, present at rest. Passive extension of the wrist and fingers meets resistance that varies from moment to moment and increases as he tries to move. Right finger extension collapses suddenly after a brief full-strength effort. Strength 5/5 elsewhere in both arms and legs; bulk and tone normal elsewhere. No tremor, no other abnormal posture, no bradykinesia.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps, triceps and brachioradialis 2+ and symmetric; knee and ankle jerks 2+. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration and joint position sense normal in both hands, including the median, ulnar and radial territories; no allodynia or hyperalgesia. He reports pain in the wrist on attempted extension.

physical_exam.right hand and wrist: The bruise has resolved. Color, temperature, sweating, hair and nail growth are the same as on the left, with no swelling, edema or trophic change.
